title: Namo
hook: a toast that never says the name, and a chant that does the same
tomorrow: the Blessed One, the Lord, the Fortunate One: which is it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the consonants: plain and breathy, d and dh, and the tongue curled back under a dot. A breath in the word. Now the first word of the homage itself.
screen: `A BREATH IN THE WORD.` → `THE HOMAGE BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Some wedding toasts never use the groom's name. Here's to him: the one who drove everyone to the airport at dawn, the one who still calls his grandmother on Sundays. Nobody in the room wonders who. The first line of the Pali homage works the same way, and it's a small puzzle once you see it. Namo tassa: homage to him. Him who? The line never says Siddhattha. It never says Gotama. Where a name should go, there's a word that only points.
screen: `A TOAST WITH NO NAME.` → `NAMO TASSA: HOMAGE TO HIM.` → `HIM WHO?`

segments.voice: Start with namo. It means homage: a bow, put into a word. Short a, long o, by the rule of two days ago. Sanskrit has the same word as namas, the one tucked inside namaste. And Vietnamese Buddhists, at home and in temple, say nam mô before a Buddha's name, as in nam mô A Di Đà Phật, homage to the Buddha Amitabha: the same old word, carried into Vietnamese by way of Chinese. One bow, many mouths. Then tassa: to him, to that one. A pointer, not a name. So the puzzle. Why point instead of name? Look at what comes next. Three titles line up behind tassa: bhagavato, the Blessed One; arahato, the worthy one; samma-sambuddhassa, the one fully awake by himself. Each ends the way tassa ends, so each points back at the same him. The chant never explains its choice. But here's one way to hear it: the homage goes to what he became, not to his family name. You'll meet one title a day for three days. By the end of the week the whole line will be yours, word by word. For now, just the first two: namo tassa. Homage to him.
screen: `NAMO: A BOW IN A WORD.` · `NAMAS, NAM MÔ: ONE OLD WORD.` · `TASSA: A POINTER, NOT A NAME.` · `THREE TITLES POINT BACK.` · then, large: `HOMAGE TO HIM.`

segments.voice: Write namo tassa on a scrap of paper, slowly, in your best letters, the way you'd letter a card. Then say it once, out loud, short a, long o, a small bow carried in two words, and let the paper sit in front of you while the breath settles.
Namo. Homage: a bow put into a word, the first sound of the Pali homage, and the same sound inside namaste and nam mô. Word four of a little Pali.
Hold on to this one: homage to him, a bow that points before it names. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Theravada temples the homage, namo tassa bhagavato arahato samma-sambuddhassa, is chanted before the refuges and precepts; in Vietnamese temples and homes, people say nam mô before a Buddha's name.

notes: Puzzle shape: the homage gives no personal name (Siddhattha, Gotama) and uses tassa plus three titles in the same case. The 'one way to hear it' reading (homage to what he became) is offered as an interpretation, not as the text's own explanation. Keeper: confirm framing.

'Vietnamese Buddhists say nam mô before a Buddha's name (nam mô A Di Đà Phật) ... by way of Chinese' (南無, a transliteration of namo): please confirm with a Vietnamese Buddhist reader; tone marks and wording.
namo = Sanskrit namas, the namas in namaste (namas + te): standard; confirm phrasing. 'Short a, long o' follows day 1428's vowel rule.
The wedding-toast image in the hook is the narrator's illustration. Amitabha gloss ('Buddha of boundless light') follows year four's Pure Land block; confirm.
Grammar simplified: tassa and the three titles share one case (dative/genitive), shown as 'each ends the way tassa ends' (-ssa / -to). Keeper: confirm this is fair for beginners.
